chunks: Interfacing an MCU with I2C targets. The question: How interface with slaves?
To use an I2C chip, you connect its two wires to the microcontroller's I2C pins, add pull-up resistors, and set the speed.
Each chip is like a small set of numbered registers that hold its settings and readings. You address the chip, tell it which register you want, then read or write bytes.
The chip's datasheet is the manual. The first thing to do when a new board first powers up is read a fixed identification register, which proves the wiring works.
Picture a filing cabinet with numbered drawers. To read a drawer, you first tell the cabinet "open drawer 3", and then you ask for its contents.
Reading several neighboring drawers in one go is faster than opening each one separately. The note on the cabinet saying what is in each drawer is the datasheet.
Targets are told apart only by address; the controller needs no extra pins as devices are added.
The addresses shown (0x48, 0x50, 0x68) are common defaults for LM75-style temperature sensors, 24-series EEPROMs and DS3231-style RTCs; always confirm in the datasheet.
Target address: the 7-bit number that picks one chip on the bus. Datasheets sometimes quote it with the read/write bit attached ("I2C address and data frames").
Register: a numbered slot in the chip holding a setting or a measurement.
Pull-up resistor: the resistor that lifts each wire to high when nobody pulls it low ("I2C pull-ups: why and how to size").
Burst read: reading several consecutive registers in a single transaction. ID register: a register with a fixed value, often called WHO AM I, used to check the connection.
Bus scan: trying every address and noting which ones answer with an ACK.
You want six consecutive registers from a chip. Reading them one at a time costs 4 bytes each: the address, the register number, the address again, and one data byte.
That is 24 bytes at 9 clock ticks, 216 ticks. One burst read is 3 overhead bytes plus 6 data bytes, 9 bytes, or 81 ticks. That is 2.
7 times faster, and all six values come from the same sample. That is the whole idea.
"All targets share SDA and SCL with one pull-up per line, and each is addressed by its 7-bit address.
In firmware I configure the MCU's I2C peripheral for 100 or 400 kilohertz, then for a sensor I write the register pointer, do a repeated START with the read bit, and read the data bytes.
I read an ID register first to prove the wiring and address, check for NACKs and timeouts, and use burst reads for efficiency."
